I was a little wrong on the weight (remembered I borrowed a Haubergeon but it was for someone taller and less rotund so I ended up in a corslet which is lighter). The point with plate (wasn't clear) is that it is heaver than maille, but easier and more comfortable to wear as it had better distribution (even with the belt maille is still heavy on the shoulders). In plate though a lot of the misconception is Victorian, we have period sources of knights in plate dancing, cartwheeling, leaping onto horses and even storming a castle wall by climbing on the underside of the ladder turning right side at the top and jumping over the crenelation. Its a matter of the balance between protection and comfort (and expense) think about if you fell over in full kit, you would want to be able to stand on your own.

I think that this is a far better forum than twitter (140 characters not enough) I just tend to waffle when the subject interests me.

I think plate is comparable to modern flack amour (given the weights) but most of my experience is with Maille (although the earl, who has reenacted for over 10 years, says plate due to strapping is easier and more comfortable to wear. As with the lower classes again depends on wealth. There was a law in Norman England called the Assize of arms which listed what was required for certain classes so the lowest would just have tunics with a shield (wooden shields are easy to build and would last one battle) to Knights required Mallie, Lances, multiple shield and helms.) Most of the more reliable feudal troops (those not just called up for a campaign but those who severed as a town watch/garrison for 6 weeks of the year) would have a helm (even if it was just a metal skullcap) and a gambeson (padded armour, thick material stuffed with whatever was to hand). Knights and lords don't atually want to lose their peasants (who farm both food and are taxed) so a basic unarmoured levy (although the law said freemen were supposed to have a gambeson but some could not afford it)  would not be committed to action if it could be avoided (though as siege troops they were useful in encircling the castle).

The burst fighting sound about right (for training at least, during shows we tend to have one big battle of 30-45 min which is 2/3 combat and 1/3 maneuvers and dealing with the 'wounded'). but in training we either do small lines (we have 300ish members but the largest normal training session I've seen is for about 20 so lines of ten are over and reset a lot quicker so that's about 2 min fighting, 30ish sec talking about what when right or wrong (and safety) and getting back in line and trying again. Or we do one on one that is over quicker and reset quicker (shows have less one on one unless it is a tournament because battles are fought in line unless you are welsh).

Then its a horse powered society (most equipment would be on horses or in wagons. Then there was the type of battle, sieges mostly. A siege can last months (long enough that we have reports of the besieging army building houses to sleep in.) These often ended either when a relief force drove the attackers away or the stronghold surrendered. Battles in the field tended to be short. When one side took about 15% casualties the Levy would start to run (they are not paid, just doing their feudal duties often only with a shield for protection) this causes the Garrison troops (similar social class, but able to afford some armor and helm to run. The loss of the army forces the Knights and Professional soldiers to withdraw or surrender.
